title: Clonal, regionally clustered spread-rather than vertical transmission-explains surges in fluoroquinolone‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni in Finnish broilers.
abstract: Campylobacter jejuni is a major zoonotic foodborne pathogen, with poultry recognized as an important reservoir for human infection. Although antimicrobial use in Finnish broiler production is minimal, sporadic increases in fluoroquinolone- and tetracycline-resistant C. jejuni have been detected. We investigated the population structure, antimicrobial resistance, and transmission pathways of C. jejuni in Finnish poultry production. A total of 333 C. jejuni isolates collected from breeder (n = 145) and broiler (n = 188) flocks during 2014-2019 were characterized using whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial resistance profiling, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), core-genome MLST (cgMLST), and phylogenomic analysis. Resistance to fluoroquinolones and tetracycline was concentrated in specific years and was strongly associated with particular lineages, especially ST-206 clonal complex (CC), whereas the predominant ST-45 CC was largely susceptible. Genomic clustering identified several resistant clones circulating among geographically proximate broiler farms, indicating regional horizontal dissemination. Resistant isolates from breeders were uncommon, and no genomic evidence supported vertical transmission of resistant strains from breeder to broiler flocks. Instead, resistance peaks were primarily attributable to clonal expansion of successful resistant lineages. Transient increases in fluoroquinolone- and tetracycline-resistant C. jejuni in Finnish broiler production were driven mainly by regional clonal horizontal spread rather than vertical transmission from breeders to broilers. These findings highlight the value of genomic surveillance for detecting and tracking antimicrobial-resistant Campylobacter lineages and support the integration of molecular epidemiology into poultry surveillance and control programmes.

title: Invasive Meningococcal Disease in Hospitalized Children in Argentina, 2020-2024: Clinical, Epidemiologic and Molecular Findings From a Multicenter Active Surveillance Study.
abstract: Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is a low-incidence but high-impact infection associated with substantial mortality and sequelae. Following MenACWY vaccine introduction into Argentina's National Immunization Program in 2017, updated data on residual disease burden are needed. A multicenter active hospital-based surveillance study was conducted in 6 pediatric sentinel units in Argentina (January 2020-December 2024) in children younger than 15 years with suspected IMD. Cases were confirmed by culture and/or polymerase chain reaction from a normally sterile body site. Hospital discharge rates were calculated per 10,000 discharges. Whole-genome sequencing and genetic Meningococcal Antigen Typing System were used to characterize strains and estimate theoretical 4CMenB coverage. Among 234,264 pediatric hospital discharges, 27 confirmed IMD cases were identified (overall rate: 1.2 per 10,000; 95% confidence interval, 0.8-1.7). Annual rates showed no consistent pattern between children younger than 2 years and those 2 years or older. The case-fatality rate was 14.8% (4/27); all deaths occurred in previously healthy children younger than 5 years and were associated with sepsis and a fulminant course (hospital stay ≤1 day). Of 20 cases with a determined capsular group, 19 (95%) were B and 1 (5%) was C; no capsular group Y or W cases were identified. Theoretical 4CMenB coverage by genetic Meningococcal Antigen Typing System was 77.3%, driven by ST-162 clonal complex predominance. IMD in Argentina continues to predominantly affect young children and is associated with elevated case-fatality amid fulminant sepsis. Serogroup B predominates in the post-MenACWY era, and high estimated 4CMenB coverage supports evaluation of serogroup B vaccination as a complementary prevention strategy.

title: HIV-1 genotypic patterns in antiretroviral-naïve and treated patients in the integrase inhibitor era in Morocco.
abstract: HIV-1 drug resistance remains a critical challenge for long-term treatment effectiveness, particularly in settings characterized by diverse viral subtypes and evolving treatment histories. We investigated the prevalence, patterns, and molecular distribution of transmitted and acquired HIV-1 drug-resistance mutations in a Moroccan cohort. A cross-sectional molecular study was performed on HIV-1-infected individuals monitored at the CVMIT in Rabat from 2024 to 2025. Demographic, clinical, and virological data were collected retrospectively from medical records. The HIV-1 pol gene was amplified and sequenced. Drug-resistance mutations were interpreted using the Stanford HIVdb v9.8 algorithm, and resistance profiles were examined by drug class, resistance level, treatment history, and viral subtype. Major surveillance drug-resistance mutations were detected in 3 of 38 ART-naïve individuals (7.9%), indicating a low but measurable burden of transmitted resistance. These mutations were limited to protease inhibitor- and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor-associated substitutions, with no major transmitted resistance detected in nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors or integrase inhibitors. Among ART-experienced patients, 11 of 26 individuals (42.3%) harbored at least one major resistance mutation. Acquired resistance was dominated by NNRTI mutations, led by K103N/S (19.2%), Y188L/H, and V106I/L (15.4%) each, followed by NRTI mutations including M184V/I (19.2%), D67N, and K70R/E (15.4%) each. Integrase inhibitor resistance was detected in three treated individuals (11.5%), involving R263K/T, Q148K, and N155H. No major protease inhibitor resistance was identified among treated patients. CRF02_AG accounted for the majority of major resistance mutations across drug classes. This study provides a detailed overview of HIV-1 DRMs in Morocco, revealing persistent NNRTI and NRTI resistance within a CRF02_AG-dominant epidemic and the emergence of INSTI mutations under DTG pressure. These findings emphasize the urgency of nationwide genotypic surveillance to guide ART management and preserve treatment efficacy.

title: Molecular epidemiological characteristics and pathogenicity of Chinese PRRSV-2 L1B sublineage strains in piglets.
abstract: PRRSV evolves through mutation and recombination during circulation, contributing to the emergence and spread of genetically diverse lineages. Among these, the PRRSV-2 L1B sublineage has been detected in multiple countries, but its molecular epidemiology and pathogenicity remain poorly characterized. We investigated the molecular epidemiology of L1B PRRSV in China and assessed its pathogenicity in piglets. L1B strains were detected in multiple Chinese provinces. Phylogenetic analysis based on the ORF5 sequences revealed that all Chinese L1B PRRSV strains cluster within the L1B sublineage of PRRSV-2. These strains harbor a 131-amino-acid discontinuous deletion (111+1+19) in the Nsp2 protein and carry cluster-associated amino acid substitutions at positions 137 and 178 of the GP5 protein. Whole-genome analysis revealed that Chinese L1B strains possess complex genetic backgrounds, likely arising from recombination between indigenous circulating strains (NADC30-like and HP-PRRSV) and the introduced L1B strains. Animal challenge experiments demonstrated that inoculation with the representative isolate TZJ2547 induced clinical symptoms including fever, coughing, and decreased feed intake, accompanied by persistent viremia, high viral RNA loads in multiple tissues, and pathological lesions in the lungs and lymphoid tissues. These findings indicate that TZJ2547 exhibits moderate pathogenicity in the challenged piglets. This study characterizes the epidemiological distribution, genomic characteristics, and recombination profile of L1B PRRSV in China. To the best of our knowledge, this study reports the first systematic pathogenicity evaluation of a Chinese L1B PRRSV isolate in piglets. Collectively, these findings provide fundamental data to inform the surveillance and control of this viral sublineage.
